item.title: Key Role of Followership in Organization Change Initiatives
item.description:
Leadership

Key Role of Followership in Organization Change Initiatives

Change occurs only if everyone is on board.

Posted May 9, 2026

Key points
  • Treating followers as active collaborators in the change process is the key to success.
  • Critical in any change initiative is clear, authentic communication from leaders and listening to followers.
  • Leaders should empower followers by reducing obstacles and rewarding proactive contributions.

This post was coauthored by Maike Kugler and Ron Riggio

It has been estimated that 70 percent of organizational change initiatives fail or fall short of expectations. Typically, when attempts at organizational transformation fail, there is finger-pointing, and the blame is placed on leadership in the majority of cases, or on the followers who either resisted the change or failed to move forward.

The real problem is that leaders and followers need to work together in all initiatives in the organization, but particularly when there is a need to change direction or implement new initiatives. In our recent article (Kugler & Riggio, 2026), we suggest that research on followers and followership needs to be incorporated into change initiatives in order for them to succeed. This means seeing followers as active contributors to change initiatives rather than recipients of finalized change decisions who potentially resist and slow down implementation.

Drawing on Kotter’s stage model for “leading change,” and incorporating research on followership, we provide some strategies for promoting successful change initiatives.

  1. Create Urgency and Voluntary Support. A key to getting organizational members on board is to not compel them to support the change program but to seek out voluntary commitment from followers by listening to their concerns and promoting authentic, two-way communication.
  2. Form a Powerful Coalition and Socially Negotiate Leader and Follower Roles. For team members to “get on board” with a change program, they need to identify as followers who support the leader and the change initiative. Based on the notion of voluntariness, true support for change initiatives and acceptance of the change leader emerge when followers freely accept their role in the process and grant the leadership role.
  3. Develop and Communicate Vision and Strategy. By communicating the change vision, leaders communicate the imaginable future and a path to get there. Thereby, they create the framework conditions for the change process in which followers can act. Hurwitz and Hurwitz (2015) point out this collaboration: “Leadership is setting the frame. Followership is creating within it.” Leaders allow followers to be active contributors to the change effort.
  4. Clarify the Follower Role in the Change Process. Leaders need to communicate the type of followership that they value in the change process. This does not mean “blind” following, but followers who understand the vision and are able to contribute to achieving it.
  5. Empower Action and Listen to Followers. Leaders need to remove obstacles and support followers’ efforts in contributing to the change strategy and process. Followers need to have the courage to speak up and let leadership know about the obstacles they encounter so that leaders can take action to eliminate or reduce them.
  6. Create Short-Term Wins and Reward Helpfulness. Leaders need to recognize and reward followers who contribute meaningfully to the change program, based on the frame created earlier. Beyond simply following leaders’ directives, followers need to be proactive and ask what they can do to be helpful in the change process. Followers who anticipate what is needed to achieve success, and then act to accomplish it, are valuable.

A focus on followers and followership and their role in the organizational change process can lead to a better understanding of the change process and why organization members might resist change, and suggest ways to best leverage followers in the change process.
